surveyDefinition.title: Running Shoes — consumer survey (Middle East & Africa)
surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A business-to-consumer (B2C) market research questionnaire about Running Shoes. Every question asks about Running Shoes specifically — not the wider market, not adjacent categories, and not any named brand. It is designed to tell a client what buyers in Middle East & Africa actually do and want in this category.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in Middle East & Africa who buy or use Running Shoes for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Adults who have bought running shoes for themselves in the past 12 months; Adults who run or jog regularly (at least once a week) and intend to buy running shoes in the next 6 months; Adults who consider running shoes as their primary athletic footwear for exercise. Excluded: Children under 18 (unless buying for themselves, but typically parent proxy); Professional athletes or elite runners (niche, not representative of mass market); Institutional buyers (e.g., gyms, schools, military) – not consumer segment; People who only buy running shoes for fashion without any running activity.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Running shoes are purchased by individual consumers for personal athletic and casual use. While some running shoes are sold to institutions (e.g., for team sports), the dominant market is everyday consumers buying for themselves.
respondentBehaviours: Engages in running or jogging at least once a week
Purchases athletic footwear for fitness or casual wear
Researches product reviews and compares brands before buying
Values performance features (cushioning, support, weight) and brand reputation
May participate in running events or use fitness apps
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income — these define who was recruited, not what is measured, so they appear in the audience definition rather than as questions.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's relationship with running — how often, in what contexts, and why they run — to frame the category. It then walks through the purchase journey: what triggers a new pair, how they research, where they buy, how often, what decides the choice, and what they typically spend. Next, it dives into their preferences: must-have features, quality cues, fit challenges, claims that matter, trade-offs, and value expectations. Finally, it assesses satisfaction with their current shoes, what drives it, frustrations, switching triggers, recommendation likelihoo

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Running Shoes in Middle East & Africa — who Adults who have bought running shoes for themselves in the past 12 months; Adults who run or jog regularly (at least once a week) and intend to buy running shoes in the next 6 months; Adults who consider running shoes as their primary athletic footwear for exercise. The consumer market for running shoes is broad, spanning casual joggers to serious amateurs. The audience is defined by personal use and purchase, with a focus on regular runners who are likely to have recent purchase intent. Excluding professional athletes keeps the survey representative of the mass consumer market.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes your current relationship with running?
options: I run regularly (at least once a week)
I run occasionally (a few times a month)
I run rarely (less than once a month)
I don't run, but I wear running shoes for other activities
I don't run and I don't wear running shoes

data.label: I run regularly (at least once a week)
I run occasionally (a few times a month)
I run rarely (less than once a month)
I don't run, but I wear running shoes for other activities
I don't run and I don't wear running shoes

questions.insight: Top response: I run occasionally (a few times a month) (32.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Mix of regular runners (Aspiring Marathoner, Serious Amateur, Heat-Adapted) plus casual/occasional runners from Budget Beginner and Family personas; some non-runners from Style-Driven and Family buyers.

questions.question: In the last 30 days, which of the following activities have you used running shoes for? Select all that apply.
questions.distributionNote: High walking and casual wear due to family and style personas; running and gym from fitness-focused personas.

questions.question: In a typical week, on how many days do you wear running shoes?
questions.distributionNote: Frequent wear driven by regular runners and casual wearers; occasional wear from family and style personas.

questions.question: How important are each of the following as reasons for your running?
questions.distributionNote: Running importance skewed moderate-to-very important due to health and fitness personas; some low importance from style and non-runner personas.

questions.question: Which ONE of the following is your main motivation for running?
options: Relieving stress or clearing my mind
Competing in races or improving my time
Spending time with friends or a running group

data.label: Relieving stress or clearing my mind
Competing in races or improving my time
Spending time with friends or a running group

questions.distributionNote: Fitness is dominant across most personas; stress relief from urban professionals and health-conscious; competition from aspiring marathoners and serious athletes.

questions.question: Who in your household is most involved in deciding which running shoes to buy?
options: I share the decision equally with someone else in my household
Someone else in my household is the main decision-maker
We each buy our own running shoes without much discussion
Not applicable – I don't buy running shoes for anyone else

data.label: I share the decision equally with someone else in my household
Someone else in my household is the main decision-maker
We each buy our own running shoes without much discussion
Not applicable – I don't buy running shoes for anyone else

questions.insight: Top response: I am the main decision-maker (60.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Most personas are independent buyers; family personas show shared decision-making, but overall individual decision-making dominates.

questions.question: In the last 12 months, for how many people in your household (including yourself) have you bought or helped buy running shoes?
options: For myself and one other person
For myself and two or more other people
Only for other people, not myself
I have not bought or helped buy running shoes in the last 12 months

data.label: For myself and one other person
For myself and two or more other people
Only for other people, not myself
I have not bought or helped buy running shoes in the last 12 months

questions.distributionNote: Family-oriented personas (Value-Seeking, Family-Focused) drive multi-person purchases; solo buyers from professional and athlete personas; some non-buyers from casual/non-runner personas.

questions.question: Which of the following situations most often prompts you to buy a new pair of running shoes?
options: My current pair is worn out or damaged
I start a new training goal or race plan
I experience discomfort, pain, or injury
I see a new model or style that I like
I find a good deal or discount

data.label: My current pair is worn out or damaged
I start a new training goal or race plan
I experience discomfort, pain, or injury
I see a new model or style that I like
I find a good deal or discount

questions.insight: Top response: My current pair is worn out or damaged (42.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Value-Seeking Family Buyer, Budget-Conscious Beginner, and Family-Focused Fitness (39% combined) drive the worn-out/damaged trigger; Aspiring Marathoner and Serious Amateur Athlete add training-goal triggers; Style-Driven Casual and Tech-Savvy Tracker add style/deal triggers.

questions.question: Before buying a new pair of running shoes, where do you typically look for information or compare options? Select all that apply.
options: In-store staff or trying shoes on in a store

data.label: In-store staff or trying shoes on in a store

questions.insight: Top response: Online reviews or comparison websites (55.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Mainstream tech adoption and high price sensitivity drive online reviews and social media; in-store still important for fit-related pain points (Value-Seeking, Health-Conscious, Family); running clubs/coaches are niche (Aspiring Marathoner, Serious Amateur).
questions.beatTitle: How they learn about running shoes

questions.question: In the last 12 months, which of the following places have you bought running shoes from? Select all that apply.
options: Online – general retailer (e.g., department store, mass merchant)
Online – directly from a brand's website
In-store – general retailer (e.g., department store, mass merchant)

data.label: Online – general retailer (e.g., department store, mass merchant)
Online – directly from a brand's website
In-store – general retailer (e.g., department store, mass merchant)

questions.insight: Top response: In-store – general retailer (e.g., department store, mass merchant) (35.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Price-sensitive personas (Value-Seeking, Budget, Family) favor general retailers and outlets; urban professionals and serious athletes favor specialist stores; online channels are used by tech-savvy and mainstream adopters.

questions.question: In the last 12 months, how many pairs of running shoes have you bought for yourself?
questions.distributionNote: Budget-conscious and family personas buy fewer pairs; serious athletes and tech-savvy buy more; overall middle-income region limits frequency.
questions.beatTitle: How often they buy running shoes

questions.question: How important is each of the following when you make your final choice of running shoes?
questions.distributionNote: Comfort, durability, and price are top drivers across personas; high price sensitivity and fit pain points push importance toward 'very' and 'extremely'.

questions.question: In the last 12 months, how much did you typically pay for a pair of running shoes for yourself?
questions.distributionNote: High price sensitivity and middle income push most purchases under $100; upper-middle personas (Urban Professional, Tech-Savvy, Serious Amateur) support the $100+ segment.

questions.question: When you buy a new pair of running shoes, how likely are you to buy the same model or brand you bought last time?
questions.distributionNote: Brand loyalty is medium overall; health-conscious older adults and serious athletes are more loyal, while value-seeking and budget buyers are more likely to switch for price.

questions.question: Which of the following features are absolutely non-negotiable for you in a running shoe? Select all that apply.
options: Arch support that fits my foot
Breathable mesh that keeps my feet cool
Durable sole that lasts more than a year

data.label: Arch support that fits my foot
Breathable mesh that keeps my feet cool
Durable sole that lasts more than a year

questions.insight: Top response: Cushioning that absorbs impact (68.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Comfort-first personas (Health-Conscious Older Adult, Urban Professional) drive cushioning/arch support; Heat-Adapted Runner and Style-Driven Casual boost breathability; Value-Seeking Family and Budget-Conscious Beginner emphasize durability.

questions.question: How do you typically judge the quality of a running shoe before buying it? Select all that apply.
options: The feel of the sole when I press on it
The materials used in the upper
The weight of the shoe in my hand

data.label: The feel of the sole when I press on it
The materials used in the upper
The weight of the shoe in my hand

questions.insight: Top response: The feel of the sole when I press on it (62.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Hands-on inspection (sole feel, stitching) is common across value and comfort personas; brand reputation matters for Urban Professional, Style-Driven, and Eco-Conscious; weight less important for most.

questions.question: Which of the following packaging features would you prefer for a new pair of running shoes? Select all that apply.
options: A box that can be reused or repurposed
No box, just a reusable bag

data.label: A box that can be reused or repurposed
No box, just a reusable bag

questions.insight: Top response: Minimal packaging with recyclable materials (42.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Eco-Conscious Millennial and Urban Professional favor recyclable/reusable options; value-focused personas are indifferent or prefer minimal to save cost; some older adults prefer standard box.

questions.question: Which of the following claims would make you more likely to choose one running shoe over another? Select all that apply.
options: Made from recycled or sustainable materials
Designed and tested by professional runners
Made in a country known for quality footwear

data.label: Made from recycled or sustainable materials
Designed and tested by professional runners
Made in a country known for quality footwear

questions.insight: Top response: Designed and tested by professional runners (45.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Performance claims appeal to athletes and tech-savvy; sustainability claims resonate with Eco-Conscious and some Urban Professionals; value-focused personas are less swayed by claims.

questions.question: If you had to compromise on one feature to keep the price of your running shoes within your budget, which would you give up first?
options: None of these – I would pay more instead

data.label: None of these – I would pay more instead

questions.distributionNote: Style is most expendable for value and performance personas; breathability is given up by some but protected by Heat-Adapted Runner; durability is last to sacrifice for family buyers.
questions.beatTitle: Trade-offs they are willing to make

questions.question: Which of the following best describes what you consider good value for a running shoe?
options: A shoe that lasts more than a year, even if it costs more
A shoe that fits comfortably and supports my feet, even if it costs more
A shoe that keeps my feet cool in hot weather, even if it costs more

A shoe that is affordable, even if I need to replace it sooner

questions.distributionNote: Comfort and durability dominate as value definitions across most personas; eco-friendly value is niche; affordability-only is significant among budget-focused personas.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied are you with your most recent pair of running shoes?
questions.distributionNote: Value-Seeking Family Buyer, Budget-Conscious Beginner, and Family-Focused Fitness (39% combined) drive dissatisfaction due to price and durability; Heat-Adapted Runner and Urban Professional add moderate satisfaction.

questions.question: How well do your current running shoes meet your needs in each of the following areas?
questions.distributionNote: Budget and family personas (39%) rate poorly on fit/durability; Health-Conscious Older Adult and Serious Amateur Athlete (13%) rate well on cushioning/support.

questions.question: Which ONE aspect of your current running shoes most needs improvement?
questions.distributionNote: Comfort/fit is top pain point across many personas; durability and breathability also strong due to Heat-Adapted Runner and family buyers.

questions.question: In the last 30 days, how often have you felt that your current running shoes were too hot or not breathable enough during or after a run?
questions.distributionNote: Heat-Adapted Runner (12%) and urban professionals (8%) report frequent heat issues; budget/family personas also experience it due to cheaper materials.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's relationship with running — how often, in what contexts, and why they run — to frame the category. It then walks through the purchase journey: what triggers a new pair, how they research, where they buy, how often, what decides the choice, and what they typically spend. storyline_notes: Added a dedicated 'fit_and_sizing' beat in preferences_expectations because fit and sizing confidence is a top pain point in the region and a critical category-specific moment for footwear.

In consumer_profile, merged 'usage_occasion' and 'need_state' into distinct beats but kept them early; 'household_role' was placed last because in the region, family involvement in purchase decisions is common but slightly more personal.
In buying_behavior, 'spend' was placed after 'decision_drivers' to keep money late, but before 'repurchase' to maintain a logical flow from the purchase event to ongoing loyalty.
In satisfaction_future_intent, 'advocacy' was placed before 'future_use' because recommending is a more direct outcome of satisfaction, while future use is more forward-looking and less sensitive.

Reflected regional realities: discovery and channel beats emphasize online research and mobile-first behavior, and the importance of local sports stores and marketplaces; breathability and heat adaptation are woven into must-haves and frict
No canonical mapping for 'fit_and_sizing' because it is category-specific and not represented in the canonical arc.
